Setup
We first load the Python libraries we need. You only have to run this cell once.

Python note. import loads a library, a toolbox written by other people. We give each library a short nickname, for example np for NumPy, so that the code stays short. Text after a # is a comment: Python ignores it, and it is there for human readers. The try ... except block runs one Colab-only line and simply skips it anywhere else.


# Libraries used in this chapter

import pandas as pd                   # data tables
import plotly.express as px           # quick charts from data tables

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each model figure gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
The model in code
Chapter 1 uses one small model to show what a model is: supply and demand in the labor market. Workers supply hours of work \(L^s\), and they offer more hours when the wage \(w\) is higher. Firms demand hours of work \(L^d\), and they hire fewer hours when the wage is higher. In the textbook’s worked exercise both relations are straight lines:
\[L^s = \bar{a}\,w + \bar{\ell} \qquad\qquad L^d = \bar{f} - w\]
A bar over a letter marks a parameter, a number the model builder chooses:

\(\bar{a}\) is the slope of labor supply: the extra hours offered when the wage rises by one dollar;
\(\bar{\ell}\) is the number of hours people would work even at a zero wage;
\(\bar{f}\) is the number of hours the firm would hire at a zero wage, a measure of its capacity.

In the code we simply write a, l and f. The wage \(w\) and employment \(L\) are the endogenous variables: the model determines them. The labor market is in equilibrium when supply equals demand, \(\bar{a}w + \bar{\ell} = \bar{f} - w\). Solving this one equation gives
\[w^* = \frac{\bar{f} - \bar{\ell}}{1 + \bar{a}} \qquad\qquad L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\]
With the textbook’s numbers (\(\bar{a} = 2\), \(\bar{\ell} = 30\), \(\bar{f} = 60\)), \(2w + 30 = 60 - w\), so \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\).

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing a=2.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. A function can return two results at once, separated by a comma.


def labor_supply(w, a=2.0, l=30.0):
    """Hours of work offered at the wage w: L^s = a w + l   (Exercise 5)."""
    return a * w + l


def labor_demand(w, f=60.0):
    """Hours of work the firm wants to hire at the wage w: L^d = f - w   (Exercise 5)."""
    return f - w


def equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0):
    """The wage and employment at which supply equals demand: w* = (f - l) / (1 + a), L* = f - w*."""
    w_star = (f - l) / (1 + a)
    L_star = labor_demand(w_star, f)
    return w_star, L_star

Let us check the functions against the textbook’s answer.

Python note. w_star, L_star = equilibrium() stores the two results of the function in two variables. An f-string such as f"w* = {w_star:.1f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.1f means “show one decimal”.


w_star, L_star = equilibrium()
print(f"Equilibrium wage       w* = {w_star:.1f}")
print(f"Equilibrium employment L* = {L_star:.1f}")
print(f"At w*, supply = {labor_supply(w_star):.1f} and demand = {labor_demand(w_star):.1f}: the market clears")

Equilibrium wage       w* = 10.0
Equilibrium employment L* = 50.0
At w*, supply = 50.0 and demand = 50.0: the market clears

The textbook draws this figure on a ratio scale: each step up the vertical axis doubles the value (1,000, 2,000, 4,000, …). Equal distances then mean equal percentage changes, so a country growing at a steady rate draws a straight line. Chapter 3 explains ratio scales in detail.

Python note. px.line draws one line per value of color=. log_y=True gives a ratio scale, and tickvals sets the numbers printed on the axis (Plotly’s own labels are hard to read on a ratio scale). On a ratio scale, the axis range is given in powers of ten: np.log10(800). The if ... else block runs one branch or the other.


TICKS = [1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000]


def six_countries(scale="ratio"):
    """Figure 1.1: GDP per person in six countries, 1870-2022 (2022 dollars)."""
    fig = px.line(long, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", hover_name="country", markers=True,
                  log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)", "country": "Country"},
                  title="Large income gaps across countries, and large gains over time")
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=TICKS, range=[np.log10(800), np.log10(90000)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 80000])
    return fig


Python note. interact calls a function and redraws its figure every time you change a control. ToggleButtons gives one button per option. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.


interact(six_countries, scale=ToggleButtons(options=["ratio", "linear"], value="ratio", description="vertical scale"));

What to notice.

In every year, the richest of the six countries has several times the income of the poorest. In 2022 the United States leads and South Africa is last.
The U.K. was richer than the United States in 1870 and 1890; by 1900 the United States was ahead.
Japan’s income fell between 1929 and 1950 (World War II) and then rose very fast: it passed South Africa in the 1950s and Argentina in the 1960s. China was almost flat until 1950 and has grown fast since, passing Argentina by 2020.
Switch to the linear scale: the lines for poorer countries are squeezed near zero, and the early growth of every country becomes invisible. That is why the textbook uses a ratio scale.


Key numbers: how much richer?
The textbook asks why the typical American is “more than 10 times richer” than a century ago and “25 times richer” than the typical Ethiopian. A wider file holds every available year for the six countries and for Ethiopia, so we can check both numbers.

Python note. .pivot(index="year", columns="iso3", values="gdppc") turns a long table back into a wide one, with the years as row labels and one column per country code. Then wide.loc[2022, "ETH"] picks one number, and us[us < x] keeps only the years in which the condition is true.


annual = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_annual.csv")
wide = annual.pivot(index="year", columns="iso3", values="gdppc")
us = wide["USA"]
print(f"U.S. 2022 / U.S. 1922:  {us[2022] / us[1922]:.1f}")
print(f"Last year with less than a tenth of the 2022 income: {us[us < us[2022] / 10].index.max()}")
print(f"U.S. / Ethiopia, 2022:  {us[2022] / wide.loc[2022, 'ETH']:.1f}")
print("U.S. / Ethiopia in other years:")
print((us / wide["ETH"]).loc[[1950, 1980, 2000, 2010, 2022]].round(1))

The 25-fold gap with Ethiopia is confirmed: in 2022 the ratio is about 25.5. The “10 times richer than a century ago” is not: in the current Maddison data, U.S. income in 2022 is about 5.8 times its 1922 level. A tenfold gap takes us back to 1879, about 140 years. (Figure 7 checks the same claim with a different data source.) Notice too that the gap with Ethiopia was much larger around 2000 (about 59 times); the textbook’s later mention of a “50-fold” gap fits those years. Ethiopia has grown fast since then. Always check a claim against the data, and say which data and which year you used.

Python note. pd.date_range(..., freq="MS") lists the first day of every month between two dates. months.isin(emp.date) is True for each month that appears in the data, and ~ turns True into False and back, so months[~ ...] keeps the months that are missing.

October 2025 is missing because the Bureau of Labor Statistics did not collect its survey during the federal government shutdown of that autumn. The chart simply joins September and November. Gaps like this are common in real data, which is why we check before we compute.

Python note. The shaded bands are the recessions. A for loop repeats the indented line once for each recession: zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough) hands over one (peak, trough) pair at a time, and fig.add_vrect shades the band between the two dates. rangeslider_visible=True adds a small copy of the chart below the axis: drag its handles to zoom in on a period.


fig = px.line(emp, x="date", y="emp_pop_ratio",
              labels={"date": "Year", "emp_pop_ratio": "Employment-population ratio (percent)"},
              title="Employment fell sharply in the 2007–09 and Covid-19 recessions")
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2))
for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
    fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
fig.update_yaxes(range=[50, 66])
fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)

What to notice.

The ratio rose from about 56 percent in the early 1960s to a peak of 64.7 percent in April 2000.
It falls in every recession (the shaded bands), but the last two falls are far deeper than the others: the 2007–09 recession and the Covid-19 collapse of spring 2020.
After 2009 the recovery was slow. After the Covid drop the ratio bounced back within two years, but it has not returned to its February 2020 level of 61.1 percent.


Key numbers: how deep was each fall?
The textbook says that the two latest recessions brought the sharpest declines in employment in more than 50 years. For each recession, we compare the ratio in the peak month with its lowest value up to two years after the trough (employment often keeps falling after a recession ends).

Python note. set_index("date") uses the dates as row labels, so ratio[:peak] keeps every month up to the peak and .iloc[-1] takes the last of them. pd.DateOffset(years=2) adds two years to a date. Each pass of the loop adds one row to the list falls, which becomes a DataFrame at the end.


ratio = emp.set_index("date").emp_pop_ratio
falls = []
for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
    at_peak = ratio[:peak].iloc[-1]
    lowest = ratio[peak:trough + pd.DateOffset(years=2)].min()
    falls.append([peak.strftime("%Y-%m"), at_peak, lowest, at_peak - lowest])

text:
Figure 3: Inflation rates in certain rich countries
Goal. Document the history of inflation in four rich economies.
The inflation rate is the percentage change in consumer prices over a year. The file has one column per economy. We rename the columns so that the chart legend is readable.

Python note. .rename(columns={old: new}) changes column names. Passing a list of columns as y=[...] makes px.line draw one line per column. add_hline draws a horizontal line, here a dashed zero line: below it, prices fall (deflation).


inflation = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-3.csv")
inflation = inflation.rename(columns={"inflation_us": "U.S.", "inflation_uk": "U.K.",
                                      "inflation_euro_area": "Euro area", "inflation_japan": "Japan"})
fig = px.line(inflation, x="year", y=["U.S.", "U.K.", "Euro area", "Japan"],
              labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Inflation rate (percent)", "variable": "Economy"},
              title="Inflation was high in the 1970s, low for 30 years, and jumped in 2021–22")
fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
fig.show()




                                
                                            




What to notice.

Inflation peaked in the 1970s: Japan at 23 percent in 1974, the U.K. at 24 percent in 1975, the United States at 13.5 percent in 1980.
From the mid-1990s to 2019, inflation was low and stable everywhere, and Japan often had deflation.
In 2021–2022 inflation jumped in all four economies. Hover over 2022 to compare them.
Click a name in the legend to hide that line; double-click to show it alone.


Key numbers: three eras of inflation
To check the caption’s story, we average inflation over eras.

Python note. pd.cut sorts each year into a bin: the years from 1960 to 1969 get the label "1960s", and so on (each bin includes its right edge). groupby("era").mean() then averages every column within each era.


inflation["era"] = pd.cut(inflation.year, bins=[1959, 1969, 1979, 1989, 2019, 2020, 2025],
                          labels=["1960s", "1970s", "1980s", "1990-2019", "2020", "2021-2025"])

text:
Figure 6: The structure of economic models
Goal. See what a model does: it takes inputs and determines outcomes.
Every economic model has the same structure. The model builder picks the inputs:

parameters, fixed numbers such as \(\bar{a}\), \(\bar{\ell}\), \(\bar{f}\), or a minimum wage set by law;
exogenous variables, inputs that may change over time in a way the model builder decides in advance, such as the number of people in the economy.

The model, a set of equations, then determines the endogenous variables, here the wage and employment. The textbook draws this as three boxes: inputs → MODEL → outcomes. Below, the boxes are live: every slider is an input, and the right box shows the outcomes the model computes.
We add one input the textbook mentions as an example of a parameter: a minimum wage. If it is below \(w^*\), it has no effect. If it is above \(w^*\), the wage equals the minimum wage, firms hire only the hours they demand at that wage, and the hours that workers offer but cannot sell are unemployment, \(L^s - L^d\). (Think of \(\bar{\ell}\) as growing with the number of people in the economy: more people offer more hours at any wage.)

Python note. fig.add_shape(type="rect", ...) draws a rectangle and fig.add_annotation(...) writes text; <br> starts a new line and <b>...</b> makes text bold. An annotation with showarrow=True draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to (x, y). max(w_star, w_min) is the larger of the two numbers. The loops run once per box and once per arrow.


def structure_of_models(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0, w_min=0.0):
    """Figure 1.6 as a live model: inputs (parameters) -> MODEL -> outcomes (endogenous variables)."""
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    w = max(w_star, w_min)                         # a minimum wage above w* sets the wage
    L = labor_demand(w, f)                         # firms hire the hours they demand at that wage
    unemployed = labor_supply(w, a, l) - L         # hours offered but not hired (zero if w = w*)
    inputs = (f"<b>INPUTS</b><br><i>parameters and exogenous<br>variables</i><br><br>supply slope a = {a}"
              f"<br>hours at zero wage l = {l}<br>demand at zero wage f = {f}<br>minimum wage = {w_min}")
    model = "<b>MODEL</b><br><br>Lˢ = a·w + l<br>Lᵈ = f − w<br>Lˢ = Lᵈ, unless<br>a minimum wage<br>is above w*"
    outcomes = (f"<b>OUTCOMES</b><br><i>endogenous variables</i><br><br>wage w = {w:.2f}"
                f"<br>employment L = {L:.2f}<br>unemployment = {unemployed:.2f}")
    fig = go.Figure()
    for x0, x1, text in [[0.0, 0.33, inputs], [0.39, 0.61, model], [0.67, 1.0, outcomes]]:
        fig.add_shape(type="rect", x0=x0, x1=x1, y0=0.12, y1=0.88, fillcolor="#ecf3fa", line=dict(color=BLUE))
        fig.add_annotation(x=(x0 + x1) / 2, y=0.5, text=text, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    for x_from, x_to in [[0.33, 0.39], [0.61, 0.67]]:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x_to, y=0.5, ax=x_from, ay=0.5, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
                           text="", showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=4, arrowcolor=GREEN)
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Inputs → model → outcomes: wage w = {w:.2f}, employment L = {L:.2f}")
    return fig


Python note. A FloatSlider chooses a number between min and max in steps of step. value is where it starts: the textbook’s numbers.

         a=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="supply slope a", style=WIDE),
         l=FloatSlider(value=30, min=20, max=40, step=5, description="hours at zero wage l", style=WIDE),
         f=FloatSlider(value=60, min=50, max=70, step=5, description="demand at zero wage f", style=WIDE),
         w_min=FloatSlider(value=0, min=0, max=20, step=1, description="minimum wage", style=WIDE));

What to notice.

With the textbook’s inputs, the outcomes are \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\), and nobody who wants to work at that wage is left out.
A minimum wage of 5 or 10 changes nothing, because it is not above the market wage. A minimum wage of 12 raises the wage to 12, cuts employment to 48, and leaves 6 hours of unemployment.
You never set the wage or employment directly: they are endogenous. You only change inputs, and the model works out the outcomes. That is what the textbook means by running an experiment with a model.

The average annual growth rate \(g\) between 1870 and 2025 is the constant rate that turns the 1870 value into the 2025 value in 155 years: \(y_{2025} = y_{1870}(1+g)^{155}\), so \(g = (y_{2025}/y_{1870})^{1/155} - 1\).

                   text=f"The average annual<br>growth rate is<br>{100 * g:.1f}% per year")
fig.show()




                                
                                            




What to notice.

The long run. Income per person rose enormously, and on a ratio scale the line is close to straight: growth of almost 2 percent a year, sustained for over 150 years.
The short run. Actual GDP (solid) moves around potential output (dashed). The Great Depression of the 1930s and the World War II boom of the 1940s are the only deviations you can see easily.
The future. The line raises an obvious question: will growth continue at the same rate?

The textbook reports $4,200 in 1870 and $76,000 in 2022, “more than a factor of 15”. Our 2022 value is close ($77,942). Our 1870 value is about 10 percent higher, because we use newer historical estimates (the Maddison Project) for the years before 1929. The rise is a factor of almost 17, and average growth is 1.9 percent a year, which the textbook rounds to 2 percent.
This series also lets us revisit the claim of Figure 1. Here, U.S. income in 2022 is about 8.1 times its 1922 level: more than the 5.8 of the Maddison data, but still short of “more than 10 times”. The two sources disagree because estimating income a century ago is hard, and they measure prices differently. When sources disagree, report the range.


The short run: the output gap
The gap between actual and potential output, in percent, is \(100 \times (\text{actual} / \text{potential} - 1)\). It is negative in recessions. The chart below plots it for every year, and the title converts the gap of the chosen year into dollars per person and for a family of four.

Python note. usgdp["gap"] = ... adds a new column, computed row by row from two other columns. usgdp[usgdp.year == year].iloc[0] picks the one row of the chosen year. px.bar draws a bar chart, and :+,.0f in an f-string shows a sign, thousands separators and no decimals.

def output_gap_chart(year=2009):

                 labels={"year": "Year", "gap": "Actual relative to potential (percent)"})

                             marker=dict(color="black", size=11)))
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[-20, 25])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{year}: gap {row.gap:+.1f}%, or {dollars:+,.0f} dollars per person "
                            f"({4 * dollars:+,.0f} for a family of four)")

Figure 8: The labor market
Goal. Draw the supply-and-demand diagram of the labor market and see how the equilibrium moves when a parameter changes.
The diagram puts employment \(L\) on the horizontal axis and the wage \(w\) on the vertical axis. Labor supply \(L^s = \bar{a}w + \bar{\ell}\) slopes up, and labor demand \(L^d = \bar{f} - w\) slopes down. They cross at the equilibrium \((L^*, w^*)\). When you move a slider away from the textbook’s values, the textbook’s curves stay on the chart as dashed gray lines, so you can see the shift.

Python note. np.linspace(0, 30, 100) creates 100 evenly spaced wages from 0 to 30. Because the wage is on the vertical axis, we compute the hours supplied and demanded at each wage and use them as x. go.Figure() starts an empty chart, and each add_trace adds one curve or set of points.


def labor_market(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0):
    """Figure 1.8: labor supply and demand, and the equilibrium (L*, w*)."""
    w = np.linspace(0, 30, 100)
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    fig = go.Figure()
    if (a, l, f) != (2.0, 30.0, 60.0):             # keep the textbook's curves for comparison
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_supply(w), y=w, name="Textbook curves (a=2, l=30, f=60)",
                                 line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_demand(w), y=w, showlegend=False, line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_supply(w, a, l), y=w, name="Labor supply, Lˢ = a·w + l", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=labor_demand(w, f), y=w, name="Labor demand, Lᵈ = f − w", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, L_star, L_star], y=[w_star, w_star, 0], mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dot")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L_star], y=[w_star], mode="markers", name="Equilibrium (L*, w*)",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=12)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Equilibrium: wage w* = {w_star:.2f}, employment L* = {L_star:.2f}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Employment, L", range=[0, 100]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Wage, w", range=[0, 30]))
    return fig

         a=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="supply slope a", style=WIDE),
         l=FloatSlider(value=30, min=20, max=40, step=5, description="hours at zero wage l", style=WIDE),
         f=FloatSlider(value=60, min=50, max=70, step=5, description="demand at zero wage f", style=WIDE));

What to notice.

With the textbook’s parameters the curves cross at \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\), the answer to the textbook’s worked exercise.
A higher \(\bar{f}\) shifts labor demand to the right: the wage and employment both rise.
A higher \(\bar{\ell}\) shifts labor supply to the right: employment rises but the wage falls.
A larger \(\bar{a}\) makes supply respond more to the wage. The supply curve gets flatter in this diagram, and it pivots around the point where the wage is zero.


Key numbers: three experiments
The formulas \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\) and \(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\) show how much each parameter moves the outcomes. With \(\bar{a} = 2\), raising \(\bar{f}\) by 3 raises \(w^*\) by \(3/3 = 1\); raising \(\bar{\ell}\) by 3 lowers \(w^*\) by 1.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Macroeconomics
text:
Summary

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole. Its big questions start from facts like these: huge income gaps across countries, deep recessions such as 2008–09 and 2020, the inflation of the 1970s and of 2021–22, high unemployment in Europe, and large U.S. budget and trade deficits.
It answers them in four steps: document the facts, build a model, compare the model with the facts, and use the model for experiments.
A model takes parameters and exogenous variables as inputs and determines the endogenous variables. In the labor-market model, \(w^* = (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})/(1 + \bar{a})\) and \(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\).
U.S. GDP per person has grown at almost 2 percent a year since 1870 (the long run), with deviations from potential output that are small except in the Great Depression and World War II (the short run).
Checking claims against the data matters: some textbook numbers hold exactly, others change with newer data.
The next chapter shows how GDP, the measure behind most of these figures, is defined and measured.

def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]

text:
The model in code
This chapter has no economic model yet. Instead it has a few accounting rules that we will use in every later chapter.
Gross domestic product (GDP) is the market value of the final goods and services produced in an economy in a given period. It can be measured in three ways that give the same number: as total production, as total spending, and as total income. On the spending side, the national income identity splits GDP by who buys the goods:
\[Y = C + I + G + NX \qquad (2.1)\]
where \(Y\) is GDP, \(C\) consumption, \(I\) investment, \(G\) government purchases, and \(NX\) net exports (exports minus imports). To compare the parts, we divide each one by GDP and get its share.
GDP measured at today’s prices is nominal GDP. It can rise because prices rise or because the economy produces more. Real GDP values production at a fixed set of prices, so it only changes when quantities change:
\[\text{nominal GDP} = \text{price level} \times \text{real GDP} \qquad (2.2)\]

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. .sum() adds up all the values of a column or a row.


def share(part, total):
    """Share of a part in a total, in percent (Tables 2.1 and 2.2)."""
    return 100 * part / total


def gdp_value(prices, quantities):
    """Value of production: price times quantity, added over all goods (nominal or real GDP)."""
    return (prices * quantities).sum()


def chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche):
    """Chain-weighted growth: the average of the Laspeyres and Paasche growth rates (Section 2.3)."""
    return (g_laspeyres + g_paasche) / 2


Table 2.4: real GDP in an economy with apples and computers
The textbook’s example economy produces only apples and computers. We store its prices and quantities in two small tables, one row per year.

Python note. pd.DataFrame({...}, index=[...]) builds a table from a dictionary: each key becomes a column and the index gives the row labels. prices.loc[2026] picks the row for 2026. Multiplying two rows, prices.loc[2026] * quantities.loc[2027], multiplies the matching columns.


prices = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [1, 2, 3], "computers": [900, 1000, 1000]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])
quantities = pd.DataFrame({"apples": [500, 500, 550], "computers": [5, 5, 6]}, index=[2025, 2026, 2027])

Nominal GDP uses each year’s own prices. Real GDP holds the prices fixed. The Laspeyres index measures the change from 2026 to 2027 with the initial (2026) prices, and the Paasche index with the final (2027) prices. Chain weighting averages the two growth rates.

Python note. An f-string such as f"{x:,.0f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text: , adds thousands separators, .0f shows no decimals and .1% shows a share as a percentage with one decimal.


for year in [2025, 2026, 2027]:

g_chain = chain_growth(g_laspeyres, g_paasche)

print(f"Growth 2026-2027: nominal {g_nominal:.1%}, Laspeyres {g_laspeyres:.1%}, "
      f"Paasche {g_paasche:.1%}, chain-weighted {g_chain:.1%}")
print(f"Chained real GDP in 2026, benchmarked to 2027: ${7650 / (1 + g_chain):,.0f}")
print(f"Inflation (nominal growth minus real growth):  {g_nominal - g_chain:.1%}")

These are the numbers of Table 2.4: real growth is 18.3 percent at 2026 prices, 17.7 percent at 2027 prices, and 18.0 percent chain-weighted. Nominal GDP grew 27.5 percent, so prices rose by about \(27.5 - 18.0 = 9.5\) percent. (The textbook gets $6,483 for chained real GDP in 2026, because it rounds the growth rate to 18.0 percent first; with the unrounded rate we get $6,482.)


Comparing countries: exchange rates and purchasing power parity
To compare GDP across countries we first convert it to a common currency with the exchange rate. But prices also differ across countries, so we then value production at common prices, which is called purchasing power parity (PPP):
\[\text{real GDP}^{\text{U.S. prices}}_{\text{China}} = \frac{\text{price level}_{\text{U.S.}}}{\text{price level}_{\text{China}}}\times\text{nominal GDP}^{\text{dollars}}_{\text{China}} \qquad (2.6)\]

def to_dollars(gdp_local, exchange_rate):
    """Convert GDP in local currency into dollars at the market exchange rate (Section 2.4)."""
    return gdp_local / exchange_rate


def at_common_prices(gdp_dollars, relative_price_level):
    """Real GDP at U.S. prices: dollar GDP divided by the price level relative to the U.S. (equation 2.6)."""
    return gdp_dollars / relative_price_level


china_dollars = to_dollars(95.1, 6.91)                  # 95.1 trillion yuan, 6.91 yuan per dollar (2019)
china_ppp = at_common_prices(china_dollars, 0.684)      # goods in China cost 68.4% of U.S. prices
print(f"China at the exchange rate: ${china_dollars:.1f} trillion, {china_dollars / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")
print(f"China at common prices:     ${china_ppp:.1f} trillion, {china_ppp / 20.6:.0%} of U.S. GDP")

Figure 3: Labor’s share of GDP
Goal. Check one of the classic “stylized facts” of macroeconomics: that labor earns about two-thirds of GDP, year after year.
The income approach splits GDP into the income earned by workers (compensation: wages, salaries and benefits) and the income earned by the owners of capital. Two parts need care. def labor_share_chart(start=1970):
    """Figure 2.3: labor's share of GDP, 1950-2025, with a straight trend line fitted from `start`."""
    after = labor[labor.year >= start]
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(after.year, after.labor_share, 1)
    fig = px.line(labor, x="year", y="labor_share", labels={"year": "Year", "labor_share": "Labor share of GDP"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), fill="tozeroy", fillcolor="rgba(22, 82, 140, 0.12)",
                      name="Labor share", showlegend=True)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=after.year, y=intercept + slope * after.year, name=f"Trend since {start}",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1950, 2025])
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0.55, 0.75])
    # slope is per year, as a fraction: x 100 for percentage points, x 10 for a decade
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Labor share: trend since {start} is {1000 * slope:+.1f} percentage points per decade")

def shade_recessions(fig):
    """Add a gray band for every NBER recession, as FRED does (Figures 2.4 and 2.5)."""
    for i in range(len(recessions)):
        fig.add_vrect(x0=recessions.start[i], x1=recessions.end[i], fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.25, line_width=0)
    return fig

    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
    shade_recessions(fig)
    if scale == "ratio":

    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 150])
    factor = deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100.iloc[-1] / deflator.gdp_deflator_2012_100.iloc[0]
    fig.update_layout(title=f"The U.S. price level rose about {factor:.0f}-fold from 1947 to 2026")

title: Chapter 2: Measuring the Macroeconomy
text:
Summary

GDP is the market value of final goods and services. Production, expenditure and income are three ways to measure it, and they give the same number (up to a small statistical discrepancy).
The national income identity \(Y = C + I + G + NX\) splits spending. In the United States, consumption is about two-thirds of GDP, and since the 1970s its rise has been matched by falling government purchases and a trade deficit.
Labor earns roughly two-thirds of income, but its share has drifted down since 1970 and is now below 60 percent.
Real GDP values production at common prices. Chain weighting averages the Laspeyres and Paasche growth rates; nominal growth is about inflation plus real growth. Comparing countries also needs common prices (purchasing power parity), which shrinks the measured gap between rich and poor countries.
The next chapter uses real GDP per person to study long-run economic growth.

def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))

text:
The model in code
This chapter has no economic model yet, but it has three tools that we will use in every later chapter. A growth rate is a percentage change: between year \(t\) and year \(t+1\) it is \((y_{t+1} - y_t)/y_t\). If a variable grows at a constant rate \(\bar{g}\) every year, starting from \(y_0\), then after \(t\) years it equals
\[y_t = y_0\,(1+\bar{g})^t \qquad (3.7)\]
This is the constant growth rule. Turning it around gives the average annual growth rate between year 0 and year \(t\):
\[\bar{g} = \left(\frac{y_t}{y_0}\right)^{1/t} - 1 \qquad (3.9)\]
Finally, the Rule of 70: a variable growing at \(g\) percent a year doubles in about \(70/g\) years.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. ** means “to the power of”, and np.log is the natural logarithm.


def constant_growth(y0, g, t):
    """Value after t years of constant growth at rate g: y_t = y0 (1 + g)^t   (equation 3.7)."""
    return y0 * (1 + g) ** t


def growth_rate(y0, yt, t):
    """Average annual growth rate between two values t years apart   (equation 3.9)."""
    return (yt / y0) ** (1 / t) - 1


def doubling_time(g):
    """Exact number of years it takes to double at growth rate g: solves 2 = (1 + g)^t."""
    return np.log(2) / np.log(1 + g)

Let us check the tools against the textbook.

Python note. An f-string such as f"{x:.1f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.1f means “show one decimal” and :.2% shows a share as a percentage.


print(f"6 billion people growing at 2% for 100 years: {constant_growth(6, 0.02, 100):.1f} billion")
print(f"Growth from $4,200 (1870) to $76,000 (2022):  {growth_rate(4200, 76000, 152):.2%} a year")
print(f"Doubling time at 2%: Rule of 70 gives {70 / 2:.0f} years; the exact answer is {doubling_time(0.02):.1f}")

Figure 4: Population over time, revisited
Goal. Learn to read a ratio scale, on which constant growth is a straight line.
At 2 percent a year, the population doubles about every 35 years (Rule of 70: \(70/2 = 35\)). It goes from 6 to 12, 24 and 48 billion. On a ratio scale, the vertical axis is labeled 6, 12, 24, 48: each step doubles the one before. Equal distances then mean equal percentage changes, so a constant growth rate draws a straight line.

def population_two_scales(n=0.02):
    """Figure 3.4: the same population path on (a) a standard scale and (b) a ratio scale."""
    T = doubling_time(n)
    t = np.linspace(0, 105, 200)
    dots = np.arange(0, 106, T)                                   # every doubling time
    L, L_dots = constant_growth(6, n, t), constant_growth(6, n, dots)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) On a standard scale ...", "(b) and a ratio scale"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Standard scale", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=L, name="Ratio scale", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=4)), row=1, col=2)
    for col in [1, 2]:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=dots, y=L_dots, name="Each doubling", mode="markers", showlegend=(col == 1),
                                 marker=dict(color="black", size=10)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Year", range=[-3, 108])
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Population L (billions)", range=[0, max(52, 1.05 * L[-1])], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(type="log", range=[np.log10(4.5), np.log10(150)], tickvals=[6, 12, 24, 48, 96], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"n = {100 * n:.1f}%: doubles every {T:.1f} years (Rule of 70: {70 / (100 * n):.1f})")
    return fig

Here are the data of Figure 2 again, now on a ratio scale, with a dashed line that grows at a constant rate. The line’s level is chosen to fit the data as closely as possible (by least squares, in logarithms).

Python note. np.log(gdp) takes the logarithm of every value at once, and .mean() averages them. On a ratio scale, a constant growth line is a straight line in logarithms, which is why we fit it there.


def ratio_scale_chart(g=0.02):
    """Figure 3.5: U.S. GDP per person on a ratio scale, with a constant-growth line at rate g."""
    years = us.year - 1870
    level = (np.log(us.gdppc) - years * np.log(1 + g)).mean()     # best-fitting starting level
    line = np.exp(level) * (1 + g) ** years
    fig = px.line(us, x="year", y="gdppc", log_y=True,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars, ratio scale)"})
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3), name="U.S. data", showlegend=True)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=us.year, y=line, name=f"Constant growth at {100 * g:.2f}%",
                             line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000], range=[np.log10(3000), np.log10(130000)])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Dashed line: {100 * g:.2f}% a year, doubling every {doubling_time(g):.0f} years")
    return fig

Goal. Count people instead of countries.

Python note. .cumsum() gives running totals: the first value, then the sum of the first two, and so on. Dividing by the total and multiplying by 100 turns them into cumulative percentages.


def cumulative_shares(year):
    """Countries sorted from poorest to richest in `year`, with the cumulative share of world population."""
    table = sample[sample.year == year].sort_values("y_rel_us_2019").copy()
    table["share"] = 100 * table.pop_millions.cumsum() / table.pop_millions.sum()
    return table


def population_distribution(year=2019):

Figure 9: U.S. population, GDP and per capita GDP
Goal. See the rules for growth rates at work.
Three rules make growth rates easy to work with. If \(x\) grows at rate \(g_x\) and \(y\) at rate \(g_y\), then

the product \(z = x \times y\) grows at \(g_x + g_y\);
the ratio \(z = x / y\) grows at \(g_x - g_y\);
the power \(z = x^a\) grows at \(a \times g_x\).

Total GDP is GDP per person times population, so its growth rate is the sum of the two growth rates. To see this, the chart divides each series by its value in the first year, so all three lines start at 1.

def growth_rules_chart(period=(1870, 2025)):

    chosen = usa.loc[start:end] / usa.loc[start]                  # every series starts at 1
    chosen = chosen.reset_index().rename(columns={"gdp_billions": "Total GDP", "gdppc": "Per capita GDP",
                                                  "population_thousands": "Population"})
    rates = 100 * growth_rate(usa.loc[start], usa.loc[end], end - start)
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y=["Total GDP", "Per capita GDP", "Population"], log_y=True,
                  color_discrete_sequence=["#e0a33b", GREEN, BLUE],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Relative to the first year (ratio scale)", "variable": "Series"})
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{start}–{end}: GDP {rates.gdp_billions:.2f}%  ≈  per capita {rates.gdppc:.2f}%"

title: Chapter 3: An Overview of Long-Run Economic Growth
text:
Summary

Sustained growth in living standards is very recent. It began about 200 years ago and spread unevenly, which produced the Great Divergence in incomes across countries.
A growth rate is a percentage change. With constant growth, \(y_t = y_0(1+\bar{g})^t\), and a variable doubles in about \(70/g\) years (Rule of 70).
On a ratio scale, constant growth is a straight line and the slope is the growth rate. U.S. GDP per person has grown at close to 2 percent a year for more than 150 years.
Growth rates differ a lot across countries, and small differences compound into huge income gaps. Counting people rather than countries, poverty has fallen dramatically, mainly because of growth in China and India.
Growth rates of products are sums, of ratios are differences, and of powers are multiples.
The next chapter builds a first model to explain why some countries are so much richer than others.

title: Chapter 4: A Model of Production
text:
The model in code
The model has one firm that rents \(K\) machines and hires \(L\) workers to make output \(Y\) (in the textbook, tons of ice cream). The production function says how much it can make:
\[Y = F(K, L) = \bar{A}\,K^{1/3}L^{2/3} \qquad (4.1)\]
\(\bar{A}\) is productivity: a higher \(\bar{A}\) means more output from the same machines and workers. The exponents add up to one, so doubling both inputs exactly doubles output (constant returns to scale). But adding capital alone raises output by less and less (diminishing marginal product). The extra output from one more machine, and from one more worker, are
\[MPK = \frac{1}{3}\,\frac{Y}{K} \quad (4.3) \qquad\qquad MPL = \frac{2}{3}\,\frac{Y}{L} \quad (4.4)\]
To let you experiment with the shape of the function, we write the exponent on capital as \(\alpha\) (“alpha”). The textbook uses \(\alpha = 1/3\), so the exponent on labor is \(1-\alpha = 2/3\).

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing A=1.0 gives an argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. ** means “to the power of”, and 1 / 3 is simply the number one third.


def production(K, L, A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Output: Y = A K^alpha L^(1 - alpha)   (equation 4.1; the textbook uses alpha = 1/3)."""
    return A * K ** alpha * L ** (1 - alpha)


def mpk(K, L, A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Marginal product of capital: MPK = alpha * Y / K   (equation 4.3)."""
    return alpha * production(K, L, A, alpha) / K


def mpl(K, L, A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Marginal product of labor: MPL = (1 - alpha) * Y / L   (equation 4.4)."""
    return (1 - alpha) * production(K, L, A, alpha) / L

Let us check the functions against the textbook. With \(\bar{A}=1\), 8 machines and 27 workers make \(8^{1/3}\cdot 27^{2/3} = 2 \cdot 9 = 18\) tons of ice cream.

Python note. An f-string such as f"Y = {Y:.2f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.2f means “show two decimals”.

print(f"MPK by a small step:  {(production(8 + small, 27) - production(8, 27)) / small:.4f}")

text:
Figure 1: The diminishing marginal product of capital
Goal. See why each extra machine adds less output than the one before.
Hold the number of workers fixed at \(L\) and draw output against capital. The curve rises, but it gets flatter: going from 1 to 2 machines adds much more output than going from 7 to 8 machines. The slope of the curve is the marginal product of capital, and it falls as \(K\) rises.

Python note. np.linspace(0, 10.4, 300) creates 300 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 10.4: the values of \(K\) at which we draw the curve. np.arange(1, 11) gives the whole numbers 1, 2, …, 10 (the end value 11 is left out). A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each value in a list.


def production_curve(A=1.0, L=70, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Figure 4.1: output against capital with labor held fixed; dots at K = 1, ..., 10."""
    K = np.linspace(0, 10.4, 300)
    dots = np.arange(1, 11)
    fig = go.Figure()
    # Dashed guides at K = 1, 2, 7 and 8, as in the textbook
    for K0 in [1, 2, 7, 8]:
        Y0 = production(K0, L, A, alpha)
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[K0, K0, 0], y=[0, Y0, Y0], mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                                 line=dict(color=GRAY, width=1, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=K, y=production(K, L, A, alpha), name="Output, Y", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=4)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=dots, y=production(dots, L, A, alpha), name="K = 1, 2, ..., 10", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10)))
    gain_1_2 = production(2, L, A, alpha) - production(1, L, A, alpha)
    gain_7_8 = production(8, L, A, alpha) - production(7, L, A, alpha)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Output gain from K = 1 to 2: {gain_1_2:.2f} tons;  from K = 7 to 8: {gain_7_8:.2f} tons",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital, K", range=[0, 10.4], dtick=1),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Tons of ice cream, Y", range=[0, 45], dtick=5))
    return fig

The textbook does not say how many workers there are. With \(\bar{A}=1\), \(L = 70\) workers reproduces its curve: \(70^{2/3} \approx 17\) tons with one machine.

text:
Figure 2: Supply and demand for capital and labor
Goal. Solve the production model and find the equilibrium prices of capital and labor.
Firms rent capital until its marginal product equals the rental price \(r\), and hire workers until their marginal product equals the wage \(w\). So the MPK and MPL curves are the demand curves for capital and labor. The supplies are fixed at \(\bar{K}\) and \(\bar{L}\), so the supply curves are vertical lines. Where supply meets demand, the markets clear:
\[r^* = \frac{1}{3}\,\bar{A}\left(\frac{\bar{L}}{\bar{K}}\right)^{2/3} \qquad\qquad
w^* = \frac{2}{3}\,\bar{A}\left(\frac{\bar{K}}{\bar{L}}\right)^{1/3}\]

Python note. make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2) creates a figure with two panels side by side, and row=..., col=... tells add_trace which panel to draw in.


def factor_markets(K_bar=1.0, L_bar=1.0, A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Figure 4.2: (a) the capital market and (b) the labor market."""
    K = np.linspace(0.3, 2.2, 200)                   # capital demanded, for the demand curve
    L = np.linspace(0.3, 2.2, 200)                   # labor demanded
    r_star, w_star = mpk(K_bar, L_bar, A, alpha), mpl(K_bar, L_bar, A, alpha)
    Y_star = production(K_bar, L_bar, A, alpha)
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("(a) The capital market", "(b) The labor market"))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=K, y=mpk(K, L_bar, A, alpha), name="Demand: MPK", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[K_bar, K_bar], y=[0.05, 0.95], name="Supply of capital", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, K_bar], y=[r_star, r_star], showlegend=False, line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[K_bar], y=[r_star], name="Equilibrium", mode="markers", marker=dict(color="black", size=12)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=L, y=mpl(K_bar, L, A, alpha), name="Demand: MPL", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=4, dash="dot")), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L_bar, L_bar], y=[0.05, 1.45], name="Supply of labor", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4, dash="dot")), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[0, L_bar], y=[w_star, w_star], showlegend=False, line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")), row=1, col=2)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[L_bar], y=[w_star], showlegend=False, mode="markers", marker=dict(color="black", size=12)), row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Capital, K", range=[0, 2.2], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Rental price, r", range=[0, 1.0], row=1, col=1)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Labor, L", range=[0, 2.2], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Real wage, w", range=[0, 1.5], row=1, col=2)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"r* = {r_star:.3f}   w* = {w_star:.3f}   |   capital gets {r_star * K_bar / Y_star:.0%} "
                            f"of output, labor {w_star * L_bar / Y_star:.0%}")
    return fig

def stock_chart(period=(1920, 2026), scale="ratio"):
    """Figure 4.3: the real S&P 500 index over a chosen period, on a ratio or linear scale."""
    start, end = period
    chosen = stocks[(stocks.year >= start) & (stocks.year <= end)]
    first, last = chosen.sp500_real.iloc[0], chosen.sp500_real.iloc[-1]
    years = (chosen.date.iloc[-1] - chosen.date.iloc[0]).days / 365.25
    growth = 100 * ((last / first) ** (1 / years) - 1)          # average annual growth, percent
    fig = px.area(chosen, x="date", y="sp500_real", log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
                  labels={"date": "Year", "sp500_real": "Real stock price index (September 2026 dollars)"},
                  title=f"{start}–{end}: the real index changed by a factor of {last / first:.1f}, "
                        f"or {growth:+.1f}% a year")
    fig.update_traces(line_color=BLUE, fillcolor="rgba(22, 82, 140, 0.15)")
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[80, 160, 320, 640, 1280, 2560, 5120, 10240])   # each tick doubles
    return fig

def predicted_income_chart(year=2023):

Figure 6: The U.S. and Chinese production functions
Goal. Bring productivity back into the model and measure it.
Countries are poorer than their capital predicts, so they must use their capital and labor less efficiently: they have a lower \(\bar{A}\). We cannot observe \(\bar{A}\) directly, but we observe everything else in equation (4.10), \(y^* = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{1/3}\). So we choose the \(\bar{A}\) that makes the equation hold exactly:
\[\bar{A} = \frac{y^*}{\bar{k}^{1/3}} \qquad (4.11)\]
This is total factor productivity (TFP). It is already in our data as the column tfp. A lower TFP shifts the whole production function down.

def compare_with_us(country="China"):
    """Figure 4.6: the U.S. production function (A = 1) and another country's (its implied TFP), 2023."""
    row = sample[sample.country == country].iloc[0]
    A, k, y = row.tfp, row.k_rel, row.y_rel
    points = pd.DataFrame({"label": ["U.S.", f"{country} with U.S. TFP", country],
                           "k": [1.0, k, k], "y": [1.0, k ** (1 / 3), y]})
    fig = px.scatter(points, x="k", y="y", text="label", hover_name="label",
                     labels={"k": "Capital per person, k (U.S. = 1)", "y": "Output per person, y (U.S. = 1)"})
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(color="black", size=12), textposition=["top center", "bottom right", "bottom right"])
    grid = np.linspace(0, 2, 300)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=grid, y=grid ** (1 / 3), name="U.S. production function, A = 1",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=grid, y=A * grid ** (1 / 3), name=f"{country}'s production function, A = {A:.2f}",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{country}: {k ** (1 / 3):.0%} of U.S. income with U.S. TFP, {y:.0%} with its own (A = {A:.2f})",
                      xaxis_range=[0, max(1.3, 1.2 * k)], yaxis_range=[0, 1.6])
    return fig

title: Chapter 4: A Model of Production
text:
Summary

The Cobb-Douglas production function \(Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}\) has constant returns to scale but a diminishing marginal product of each input on its own.
In equilibrium, capital and labor are fully employed, and their prices equal their marginal products. Capital earns one-third of output and labor two-thirds, whatever the amounts of capital and labor.
Per person, the model says \(y^* = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{1/3}\). With equal productivity, it predicts much smaller income gaps than we see, because of diminishing returns to capital.
Measured as the residual that makes the model fit, TFP differs enormously across countries and explains most of the gap between rich and poor, roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of it.
The production model takes capital as given. The next chapter, on the Solow model, explains where capital per person comes from.

def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):

title: Chapter 5: The Solow Growth Model
text:
The model in code
The Solow model has two key equations. Output per person \(y_t\) depends on capital per person \(k_t\) with diminishing returns:
\[y_t = \bar{A}\,k_t^{1/3} \qquad (5.6)\]
and capital per person changes each year by net investment, which is new investment minus depreciation:
\[\Delta k_{t+1} = \bar{s}\,y_t - \bar{d}\,k_t \qquad (5.7)\]
A bar over a letter marks a parameter, a number we choose from outside the model:

\(\bar{A}\) is productivity;
\(\bar{s}\) is the investment rate, the share of output that is saved and invested;
\(\bar{d}\) is the depreciation rate.

In the code we simply write A, s and d.
The economy stops changing when investment exactly replaces the capital that wears out, \(\bar{s}y^* = \bar{d}k^*\). Solving for \(k^*\) gives the steady state:
\[k^* = \left(\frac{\bar{s}\bar{A}}{\bar{d}}\right)^{3/2} \quad (5.8) \qquad\qquad
y^* = \left(\frac{\bar{s}}{\bar{d}}\right)^{1/2}\bar{A}^{3/2} \quad (5.9)\]

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing A=1.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. ** means “to the power of”.


def output(k, A=1.0):
    """Output per person: y = A k^(1/3)   (equation 5.6)."""
    return A * k ** (1 / 3)


def steady_state_k(s, d, A=1.0, n=0.0):
    """Steady-state capital per person: k* = (s A / (n + d))^(3/2)   (equation 5.8; n is used in Figure 11)."""
    return (s * A / (n + d)) ** (3 / 2)

Let us try the functions with the values used throughout this chapter: \(\bar{s}=0.4\), \(\bar{d}=0.1\), \(\bar{A}=1\).

Python note. An f-string such as f"k* = {k_star:.2f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.2f means “show two decimals”.


k_star = steady_state_k(s=0.4, d=0.1)
y_star = output(k_star)
print(f"Steady-state capital per person k* = {k_star:.2f}")
print(f"Steady-state output per person  y* = {y_star:.2f}")
print(f"Check with equation (5.9):      y* = {(0.4 / 0.1) ** 0.5 * 1.0 ** 1.5:.2f}")

Steady-state output per person  y* = 2.00

title: Chapter 5: The Solow Growth Model
text:
Figure 1: The Solow diagram
Goal. See why the economy moves toward the steady state \(k^*\) from any starting point \(k_0\).
The Solow diagram plots the two parts of equation (5.7) against capital per person \(k\):

investment \(\bar{s}y = \bar{s}\bar{A}k^{1/3}\), which is a curve because of diminishing returns;
depreciation \(\bar{d}k\), which is a straight line.

When investment is above depreciation, net investment is positive, so capital grows. When it is below, capital shrinks. Where the two cross, capital stops changing: that point is the steady state \(k^*\).

Python note. np.linspace(0, 20, 200) creates 200 evenly spaced numbers from 0 to 20: the values of \(k\) at which we draw the curves. go.Figure() starts an empty chart, and each add_trace adds one curve or set of points. We fix the axis ranges so that you can see the curves move when a parameter changes.


def solow_diagram(s=0.4, d=0.1, A=1.0, k0=2.7):
    """The Solow diagram (Figure 5.1): investment s*y and depreciation d*k against k."""
    k = np.linspace(0, 20, 200)                     # capital per person on the x-axis
    k_star = steady_state_k(s, d, A)
    net = s * output(k0, A) - d * k0                 # net investment at the starting point
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=s * output(k, A), name="Investment, s·y", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=d * k, name="Depreciation, d·k", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[k0, k0], y=[d * k0, s * output(k0, A)], name="Net investment at k0",
                             mode="lines", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=5)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[k_star], y=[d * k_star], name="Steady state", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=11)))
    # An arrow on the x-axis: capital moves from k0 toward k*
    fig.add_annotation(x=k_star, y=0.05, ax=k0, ay=0.05, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
                       showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor=GREEN)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"k* = {k_star:.2f}   |   net investment at k0 = {k0}: {net:+.3f}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, 20]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Investment and depreciation", range=[0, 2]))
    return fig

Now the interactive version. Move the sliders and watch where the curves cross.

Python note. interact turns each argument of a function into a slider and calls the function again every time you move one. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

At \(k_0 = 2.7\) the green bar points up: investment exceeds depreciation, so capital rises toward \(k^* = 8\).
Drag \(k_0\) above \(k^*\) and the net investment becomes negative, so capital falls back toward \(k^*\).
Raising \(\bar{s}\) or \(\bar{A}\) lifts the investment curve and moves \(k^*\) to the right. Raising \(\bar{d}\) makes the depreciation line steeper and moves \(k^*\) to the left.

section: Figure 2: The Solow diagram with output
text:
Figure 2: The Solow diagram with output
Goal. Add the production function to the diagram and read off output, investment and consumption in the steady state.
Every unit of output is either consumed or invested. So consumption per person is the gap between the output curve and the investment curve: \(c = y - \bar{s}y = (1-\bar{s})\,y\).

def solow_with_output(s=0.4, d=0.1, A=1.0):
    """The Solow diagram with output (Figure 5.2): y, s*y and d*k, with consumption at k*."""
    k = np.linspace(0, 20, 200)
    k_star = steady_state_k(s, d, A)
    y_star = output(k_star, A)
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=output(k, A), name="Output, y", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=s * output(k, A), name="Investment, s·y", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=d * k, name="Depreciation, d·k", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    # Consumption in the steady state: the gap between y* and s*y*
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[k_star, k_star], y=[s * y_star, y_star], name="Consumption, c*",
                             mode="lines+markers", line=dict(color="black", width=4)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"y* = {y_star:.2f}   investment = {s * y_star:.2f}   consumption c* = {(1 - s) * y_star:.2f}",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, 20]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Output, investment and depreciation", range=[0, 3]))
    return fig

What to notice.

The black bar is steady-state consumption. A higher \(\bar{s}\) raises \(y^*\), but it also means a larger share of output is invested rather than consumed.
Productivity \(\bar{A}\) moves both the output curve and the investment curve. That is why it has such a large effect on \(y^*\): the exponent on \(\bar{A}\) in equation (5.9) is \(3/2\).

Figure 4: An increase in the investment rate
Goal. Run the first experiment. The economy sits in its steady state, and then the investment rate rises permanently from \(\bar{s}\) to \(\bar{s}'\).
The investment curve \(\bar{s}y\) rotates upward, and the depreciation line does not move. At the old \(k^*\), investment now exceeds depreciation, so capital accumulates until the new steady state \(k^{**}\).

def increase_in_s(s=0.4, s_new=0.6, d=0.1, A=1.0):
    """Figure 5.4: the investment curve shifts up when s rises to s_new."""
    k = np.linspace(0, 25, 200)
    k_old, k_new = steady_state_k(s, d, A), steady_state_k(s_new, d, A)
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=s * output(k, A), name="Old investment, s·y",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=s_new * output(k, A), name="New investment, s'·y", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=d * k, name="Depreciation, d·k", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[k_old, k_new], y=[d * k_old, d * k_new], name="k* (old) and k** (new)",
                             mode="markers", marker=dict(color="black", size=11)))
    fig.add_annotation(x=k_new, y=0.08, ax=k_old, ay=0.08, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
                       showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor=GREEN)
    fig.update_layout(title=f"k* = {k_old:.2f}  →  k** = {k_new:.2f}   (k**/k* = {k_new / k_old:.2f})",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, 25]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Investment and depreciation", range=[0, 2.5]))
    return fig

Figure 5: Output after an increase in the investment rate
Goal. Follow output per person year by year after the investment rate rises in 2020.
The Solow model cannot be solved with a formula for every year, but a computer can simply apply equation (5.7) one year at a time. This is called a simulation. The function below starts the economy in its old steady state and changes the parameters in change_year. We will reuse it in Figures 7 and 13.

Python note. A for loop repeats the indented lines once for each year. if ... else chooses between two cases. y_path.append(...) adds one more number to the end of a list.


def simulate(s_old=0.4, s_new=0.4, d_old=0.1, d_new=0.1, destroyed=0.0,
             A=1.0, change_year=2020, first_year=2000, last_year=2100):
    """Output per person, year by year, when something changes in change_year.

    The economy starts in its old steady state. From change_year on, the investment rate is s_new and
    the depreciation rate is d_new; in change_year a share `destroyed` of the capital stock is lost.
    """
    years = np.arange(first_year, last_year + 1)
    k = steady_state_k(s_old, d_old, A)                # start in the old steady state
    y_path = []
    for year in years:
        if year < change_year:
            s, d = s_old, d_old
        else:
            s, d = s_new, d_new
        if year == change_year:
            k = k * (1 - destroyed)                    # an earthquake or a war destroys capital
        y_path.append(output(k, A))
        k = k + s * output(k, A) - d * k               # capital accumulation, equation (5.7)
    return years, np.array(y_path)

Figure 11: The Solow diagram with population growth
Goal. Add population growth at rate \(\bar{n}\) and see what changes.
Every year new workers arrive, and they must be equipped with capital too. Part of investment is therefore used up just to keep capital per person constant. The capital accumulation equation becomes
\[\Delta k_{t+1} = \bar{s}y_t - (\bar{n}+\bar{d})\,k_t \qquad (5.15)\]
so population growth works like extra depreciation. The steady state is \(y^* = \bar{A}^{3/2}\left(\frac{\bar{s}}{\bar{n}+\bar{d}}\right)^{1/2}\) (5.16).

def solow_with_population(s=0.4, n=0.02, d=0.08, A=1.0):
    """Figure 5.11: investment s*y against the line (n + d)*k."""
    k = np.linspace(0, 20, 200)
    k_star = steady_state_k(s, d, A, n=n)
    y_star = output(k_star, A)
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=s * output(k, A), name="Investment, s·y", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=(n + d) * k, name="(n + d)·k", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=d * k, name="d·k (no population growth)", line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[k_star], y=[(n + d) * k_star], name="Steady state", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=11)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"k* = {k_star:.2f}   y* = {y_star:.2f}   |   total GDP grows at n = {100 * n:.1f}% a year",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, 20]),

Goal. See what happens when a disaster destroys part of the capital stock but leaves the population and the parameters unchanged.

def earthquake_diagram(destroyed=0.5):
    """Figure 5.12: an earthquake moves the economy from k* to k0 = (1 - destroyed) k*; no curve shifts."""
    s, d, A = 0.4, 0.1, 1.0                              # the parameters do not change
    k = np.linspace(0, 14, 200)
    k_star = steady_state_k(s, d, A)
    k0 = (1 - destroyed) * k_star
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=output(k, A), name="Output, y", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=s * output(k, A), name="Investment, s·y", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=d * k, name="Depreciation, d·k", line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[k_star, k0], y=[output(k_star, A), output(k0, A)], name="Output before and after",
                             mode="markers", marker=dict(color="black", size=11)))
    fig.add_annotation(x=k0, y=0.15, ax=k_star, ay=0.15, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
                       showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="crimson", text="earthquake")
    fig.update_layout(title=f"k falls from {k_star:.1f} to {k0:.1f};  output falls to {output(k0) / output(k_star):.0%} of y*",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, 14]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Output, investment and depreciation", range=[0, 2.7]))
    return fig

What to notice.

Losing half of the capital stock lowers output by only about 21 percent, because \((1/2)^{1/3} \approx 0.79\). Diminishing returns work in reverse: the units of capital that are lost were the least productive ones.
The steady state does not change, so the economy eventually returns to exactly where it started.

Goal. Follow the recovery year by year. We reuse simulate, now with a destroyed share of capital in 2020.

def output_after_earthquake(destroyed=0.5, scale="ratio"):
    """Figure 5.13: output per person over time when an earthquake destroys capital in 2020."""
    years, y = simulate(destroyed=destroyed)
    back = years[(years > 2020) & (y >= 0.99 * y[0])]          # years in which output is back within 1% of y*
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=years, y=y, name="Output per person", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[2000, 2100], y=[y[0], y[0]], name="Steady state y*", mode="lines",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")))
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(type="log", range=[np.log10(0.8), np.log10(2.2)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0.8, 2.2])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Output falls by {100 * (1 - y[20] / y[0]):.0f}% in 2020 and is back within 1% of y* in {back[0]}",
                      xaxis_title="Year", yaxis_title="Output per person, y")
    return fig

Output drops at once in 2020 and then grows back. Growth is fastest right after the shock, when the economy is furthest below its steady state.
Studies of cities rebuilt after wars, such as Hiroshima, Nagasaki and the bombed provinces of Vietnam, find this kind of recovery within one generation.

title: Chapter 5: The Solow Growth Model
text:
Summary

The Solow model makes capital endogenous. Capital grows when investment \(\bar{s}y\) exceeds depreciation \(\bar{d}k\), and it stops growing at the steady state \(k^* = (\bar{s}\bar{A}/\bar{d})^{3/2}\).
Because of diminishing returns to capital, capital accumulation cannot be the engine of long-run growth: output per person settles at a constant \(y^*\).
Changes in \(\bar{s}\), \(\bar{d}\) or \(\bar{n}\) change the level of the steady state. The economy then grows or shrinks for a while, and fastest when it is farthest from the steady state (the principle of transition dynamics).
The data agree with the model on capital-output ratios and on catch-up within the OECD. But for the world as a whole, productivity differences, not investment, explain most of the gap between rich and poor countries.
The next chapter looks for the engine of long-run growth: new ideas.
